newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cattlemen criticize new mad cow book.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cattlemen criticize new mad cow book.

text.p: The National Cattlemen's Beef Association said a new book suggesting that the U.S. food supply is vulnerable to mad cow disease is based on faulty science.
The book, "Deadly Feasts" by Pulitzer Prize-winning author Richard Rhodes, is being heavily promoted in a book tour of several U.S. cities.

"This is really just throwing fears out there that are unfounded when we've got lots of data to show that neither BSE or mad cow disease is present," Gary Weber of the National Cattlemen's group said in an interview. "He's got a very clear anti-government bias, and he's not willing to tell the whole story."

The book suggests that a native strain of mad cow disease, known to scientists as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), may be present in some U.S. elk, deer and mink. The author also contends that proposed Food and Drug Administration rules to ban the use of leftover cattle remains in making animal feed do not go far enough to protect the public.

The cattlemen's group issued a one-page statement summarizing several key points from the book and offering evidence to the contrary. The trade group contends that Rhodes failed to provide scientific evidence for his claims, and neglected to interview government scientists who have monitored the disease for the past 10 years.
More than a dozen human deaths were blamed on last year's mad cow disease outbreak in Britain.
